content:
To finish with the declensions, all that remains for us is to look at those of the PRONOUNS and PRONOUN-ADJECTIVES. Their only difficulty lies in their variety, but you will quickly see that it is easy to retain the various forms that follow, for the corresponding words are very commonly used. We remind you also that in English certain pronouns have kept part of their declension (e.g.: *I, me, my*), and that this seems quite natural to us.

## 1. The solus type

Let us first consider a perfectly regular case, the (indefinite) pronoun-adjective solus, *alone*.

| | Singular | | | Plural | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | *Masculine* | *Feminine* | *Neuter* | *Masculine* | *Feminine* | *Neuter* |
| nom. | sol**us** | sol**a** | sol**um** | sol**i** | sol**ae** | sol**a** |
| acc. | sol**um** | sol**am** | sol**um** | sol**os** | sol**as** | sol**a** |
| gen. | sol**ius** | sol**ius** | sol**ius** | sol**orum** | sol**arum** | sol**orum** |
| dat. | sol**i** | sol**i** | sol**i** | sol**is** | sol**is** | sol**is** |
| abl. | sol**o** | sol**a** | sol**o** | sol**is** | sol**is** | sol**is** |

You will notice that this declension differs from that of the adjectives of the 1st class (bon**us**, bon**a**, bon**um**) only by the genitive singular in -ius for all three genders and the dative singular in -i, likewise for all three genders. You will remember that it is the fourth declension that has the genitive singular in -us (not in -ius) and the 3rd that has the dative singular in -i.

Like solus are declined unus, -a, -um, *one (alone)*; nullus, -a, -um, *no (none)* and totus, -a, -um, *whole*.

## 2. Variations on the same model

Replacing -us by -er, -a by -(e)ra, -um by -(e)rum, we decline alter, -era, -erum, *the one, the other (of a group of two), the second*; neuter, -tra, -trum, *neither the one nor the other*, and uterque, utraque, utrumque, *the one and the other* (que does not change).

E.g.: acc. m. alterum; f. alteram; n. alterum; gen. alterius, for all three genders; dat. alteri; abl. altero; and plural following the declension of the 2nd class of adjectives.

Replacing -us by -e in the masculine, we decline the demonstrative ipse, ipsa, ipsum, *(self), same*; ipse veni, *I came myself, I came in person*.

Replacing in addition -um by -ud in the neuter, we decline: iste, ista, istud (acc. sg. istum, istam, istud), demonstrative pronoun-adjective of the 2nd person; likewise ille, illa, illud, which corresponds to the 3rd person (vid. L. 44, N. 2).

Likewise is, ea, id, demonstrative pronoun-adjective of reference (the person or thing just spoken of) differs from the preceding only by the forms of the nominative singular masculine and neuter and the accusative singular neuter (acc. sg. eum, eam, id). In the plural, the forms ei (nominative m.) and eis (dat. and abl. of all three genders) are sometimes written ii and iis. Finally the genitive of all three genders is indeed eius if the classical letters are used, but ejus with modern letters, which changes nothing in pronunciation since j = consonantal i.

Like is, ea, id is declined idem, eadem, idem, *the same* (the person or thing just spoken of), reinforcing the preceding with the indeclinable particle -dem.

Finally hic, haec, hoc, demonstrative pronoun-adjective of the 1st person (vid. L. 44, N. 2), is graced with a -c that comes and goes, which also appears in the accusative singular hunc, hanc, hoc (note also -n instead of -m); disappears in the genitive hujus; reappears in the dative huic and the ablative hoc, hac, hoc, and only shows itself in the plural in the nominative and accusative neuter: haec (m. hi, hos, f. hae, has).

## 3. The interrogative and the relative

After the declension of the solus type, let us now look at the other branch of the family.

We already know the personal pronouns well enough not to waste time on them. Just know that only the first two persons, ego, tu; pl. nos, vos, are represented in all cases. The 3rd exists only in the reflexive form (acc. se, gen. sui, dat. sibi, abl. se), which has no nominative and serves for the singular as well as the plural.

Let us rather review the declension of the interrogative pronoun-adjective.

| | Singular | | | Plural | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | *Masculine* | *Feminine* | *Neuter* | *Masculine* | *Feminine* | *Neuter* |
| nom. | quis\* | quae | quid\* | qui | quae | quae |
| acc. | quem | quam | quid\* | quos | quas | quae |
| gen. | cujus | cujus | cujus | quorum | quarum | quorum |
| dat. | cui | cui | cui | quibus | quibus | quibus |
| abl. | quo | qua | quo | quibus | quibus | quibus |

This declension is somewhat closer to the 3rd declension (acc. m. sg. and dat. abl. pl. of all three genders). One will also notice that the q becomes c in the genitive and dative singular and that the nominative and accusative plural neuters are -ae instead of -a (as in haec).

The RELATIVE pronoun-adjective qui, quae, quod differs from the preceding only in the forms of the nominative singular (m. and n.) and the accusative singular neuter (marked with an \* in the table above).

N.B. — Quis becomes qui and quid becomes quod for the INTERROGATIVE ADJECTIVE; e.g.: quis (pr.) venit? but qui (adj.) homo venit? Likewise quid (pr.) vidisti? but quod (adj.) animal vidisti?

## 4. Compound pronoun-adjectives

Other pronoun-adjectives are declined on these models. One obtains them, for example, by adding to a pronoun-adjective:

- an indeclinable particle; e.g.: aliquis, aliqua, aliquid, *someone, something*; quidam, quaedam, quiddam (quoddam for the adjective), *a certain man, a certain thing*;
- another pronoun-adjective (plus an indeclinable particle); e.g.: unusquisque, unaquaeque, unumquidque (unumquodque for the adj.), *each one, each*; unus is declined like solus (or may even be omitted: quisque, quaeque, quidque, *each one*); quis is also declined as above and que does not change.

This arsenal of words already seems imposing to you, and yet we have not shown you all those that can be formed by the method indicated in 4 above. You will see through usage that all this is much less frightening and much more practical than the display we have just treated you to would suggest.

And remember, too, that you have already made serious progress. Apart from a few exceptions and a few peculiarities, such as the Greek declensions, which we will not dwell on, we have already met all the important declinable forms. All that remains for us is to get to know them better through usage, and perhaps also through a few revisions in the course of which you may begin to make use of the grammatical appendix.

## The second wave

And now we are going to begin the ACTIVE PHASE of our study: the second wave.

Indeed, up to now, we have only asked you to listen, read and repeat the texts of the lessons and exercises passively. As for the notes and revisions, we have already told you that they were made to help you and not to torment you.

For the following lessons, you need only continue in the same way: read the text a first time comparing it with the English and consulting the notes, then practise repeating each paragraph after reading it; finally, if necessary, begin these exercises again until the text has become familiar to you. And do not forget that the recordings will make your repetitions easier.

This is what we are now asking of you: when you have finished the 50th lesson, go back to the 1st lesson (*Latine loqueris?*); read it and first repeat it like an ordinary lesson (or better, listen to the recording). Then, hide the Latin text and try to recover it sentence by sentence from the English text; this exercise is best done aloud or in writing, the one not preventing the other.

N.B. — If the principle of the second wave seems to you to raise difficulties, reread the introduction.
